newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia threatens to bankrupt big tax debtor.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia threatens to bankrupt big tax debtor.

text.p: Russia's cash-strapped government, determined to squeeze overdue taxes out of recalcitrant corporate debtors, threatened on Tuesday to drive one of its biggest oil producers, Nizhnevartovskneftegaz, into bankruptcy.

But it accepted plans by another big oil producer, Noyabrskneftegaz, to issue possibly millions of dollars of new shares to pay off the debt, a spokesman for Finance Minister Anatoly Chubais told Reuters.
The two moves underscored the government's determination to make enterprises pay their tax bills, just as Moscow launches a second wave of privatisation in the oil sector.

Chubais told a government commission that AOOT Nizhnevartovskneftegaz would not be allowed to restructure its tax debt and the government had decided to initiate bankruptcy proceedings against it, spokesman Andrei Trapeznikov said.
"It was decided to start bankruptcy proceedings and send a corresponding petition to the arbitration court," he said.

Chubais's announcement coincided with another by the privatisation authorities that Russia was seeking bids for 40 percent of Tyumenskaya Neftyanaya Kompaniya (TNK) or Tyumen Oil, a vertically integrated oil company whose main production unit is Nizhnevartovskneftegaz.

The decision by Chubais, who is also First Deputy Prime Minister in charge of economic policy, does not mean that Nizhnevartovskneftegaz will definitely be declared bankrupt, since Moscow has been loathe to liquidate companies.
But shares in the oil company, based in Western Siberia, one of Russia's main oil-producing regions, fell sharply on the news, to close at $8.55 after Monday's closing $10.00.

President Boris Yeltsin's new reformist cabinet has been driven into tough measures against companies not paying taxes by a slump in revenues, which were running at only 65 percent of budgeted levels in the first four months of this year.
That has forced the government to bring in proposals to slash planned spending, sparking a potentially destabilising fight with the opposition-dominated parliament.
The State Duma lower house, which turned down proposed cuts in welfare spending on Tuesday, is to debate the overall spending cuts plan on Wednesday.

Coupled with plans to restructure inefficient monopolies, the tax drive is already paying off. Gas monopoly Gazprom, which earlier this year owed the government a total of 14.8 trillion roubles ($2.57 billion), has now paid off all its federal taxes, although it still owes money to other bodies such as the state pension fund, government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said.
The government has proposed that the biggest tax debtors agree a schedule of repayments, guaranteed by an issue of shares or asset-backed bonds held as collateral by the authorities.
If the debtors default on the scheduled payments, the government can sell the securities.

The commission heard that plans for the biggest tax debtor, loss-making car producer AvtoVAZ, and Norilsky Gorno-Metallurgichesky Kombinat (NGMK), the flagship plant of Norilsk Nickel, one of the world's biggest producers of non-ferrous metals, to issue controlling stakes of new shares to the government had been approved.

Plans for asset-backed bond issues by another two oil producers, Yuganskneftegaz and Samaraneftegaz, both subsidiaries of the YUKOS oil group controlled by Bank Menatep, were approved by the commission.

The commission also agreed to let Noyabrskneftegaz, which is mostly owned by the OAO Sibirskaya Neftyanaya Kompaniya (Sibneft) oil group, sell shares to pay off the 1.47 trillion roubles in taxes it owed as of May 1.
But the commission said it would not allow Nizhnevartovskneftegaz to restructure its debt.
"We cannot confirm that this company is in a position to pay the current payments," Interfax news agency quoted Mostovoi as saying.
It is unclear how the move will affect the sale of the 40 percent stake in Tyumen Oil, which owns 38 percent of Nizhnevartovskneftegaz, including 51 percent of voting shares.
The government, which is accepting bids until July 16, wants investment of at least $160 million in Tyumen Oil over two years. The stake itself costs 145 billion roubles. ($=5,760 roubles)
